messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh is a 72-year-old nanny, a job he took after retiring from a decades-long career in restaurant work. He is married and lives with his wife in a small apartment, but his days are spent caring for the toddler of a young professional couple. For most of his life, Minh has carried a secret he never speaks of: the physical abuse he suffered at the hands of his former romantic partner. The beatings occurred over several years, always in the dark of their shared bedroom after he had expressed any frustration or anger. He learned that showing emotion only made the violence worse, so he taught himself to suppress all anger completely, to avoid any circumstance that might feel like that dark room, and to steer clear of anything he considered stressful. Now, nearly five decades later, these strategies have become automatic, but they no longer keep the past at bay.

When memories of the abuse surface—often triggered by a sudden darkening of a room or the unexpected movement of a child running past him—Minh feels the same terror he felt then. His body stiffens, his arms draw in as if he is bracing for a blow. The memory feels alien, as though it belongs to someone else, yet the physical reenactment is undeniable: his legs lock, his shoulders hunch, and for a moment he is back in that bedroom. This terror directly fuels his hypervigilance. He startles at the slightest noise—a dropped spoon, a creaking door—and cannot relax even when he knows he is safe. At work, the toddler’s sudden grabs or the mother walking into the room unexpectedly send his heart racing. Each startle reinforces the memory, because his body remembers the position he was in when the abuse happened, and he finds himself recreating that posture even as he tries to calm down.

The threat response, in turn, strengthens his maladaptive strategies. After a startle episode, Minh becomes even more determined to suppress any flicker of irritation or annoyance. He avoids going into the child’s dark room at night, asking the mother to handle bedtime instead. He declines to take the child to the park if the weather is overcast, because dim light reminds him of the bedroom. He tells himself that if he can just control his environment perfectly, the memories will stay away. But the opposite is true: the more he avoids, the more the memories intrude. When he deliberately swallows his anger at a misbehaving child, the effort of suppression itself triggers a vivid flashback—his jaw clenches, his vision narrows, and he feels the cold floor beneath his back. The memory returns stronger, feeding the cycle.

Over the months, this loop has tightened. Minh has become increasingly isolated at work, communicating only in short sentences, avoiding any interaction that might feel confrontational. His wife has noticed that he jumps at her touch and spends his evenings sitting stiffly in the living room, unable to relax. She urged him to see a therapist after he broke down crying during a thunderstorm, unable to explain why the sound of rain against the window terrified him. What finally brought Minh to the clinic was a single moment: the toddler accidentally knocked over a lamp, plunging the room into darkness. Minh dropped to his knees, his arms wrapped around his head, and stayed that way for several minutes. The mother found him there. He could not bring himself to explain. He is most afraid that if he lets himself talk about the abuse, the anger he has buried for so long will explode and destroy everything he has built. But he is also exhausted, and he hopes that maybe, at last, he can learn to live without the constant vigilance.
